source.citation: Bruening DA, Reynolds RE, Adair CW, Zapalo P, Ridge ST (2018). A sport-specific wearable jump monitor for figure skating. PLoS One 13(11), e0206162. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0206162. Table 1, 'Video', all isolated jumps.
source.notes: Open access; read in the full text (PMC6248918), so primary outright. Flight time from high-speed video, take-off = the frame the take-off toe first lifted, landing = the frame the landing toe first touched: 0.44 +/- 0.060 s (mean +/- SD) over 59 isolated multi-revolution jumps, mostly single axels and doubles with a few triples, by 7 competitive skaters aged 12-27 (6 F, 1 M), Juvenile to Senior. Successfully landed jumps only: 0.44 +/- 0.058. u_m is the reported SD of the jumps. One-sided (fidelity-gate §4.3 O5): the model has no effort input, so the case asks only that the model can fly at least this long. Script copied unchanged from flight-residual-full-jump-moves, written in an earlier session, so no input was chosen for this case. Reference skater: the paper gives no masses. A pooled mixed-level population standing in for the reference skater: L1. Also in the paper, not cased: peak in-air rotation 1,273 deg/s for doubles and 1,465 for triples, means with no spread, and no gate observable for in-air rate yet. First run, 2026-09-22: 0.592 s, a pass. Noted, not acted on: that is about 2.5 SD above this population's mean, which a one-sided case cannot judge; a two-sided check needs footage of specific jumps.
